For nine days three jars had stood in a row on the kitchen windowsill, each with a wooden skewer hanging into it from a clothespin, and for nine days my sister Hana had measured them. Every evening at seven she lifted the skewers out one at a time, held them against a ruler, and wrote the lengths of the sugar crystals in a green notebook. The project was due at the science fair on Thursday morning. Its title, lettered on a poster board that leaned against the hallway wall, was "How Fast Do Sugar Crystals Grow?"

On Wednesday I came home before she did. The kitchen was cold, and the crystals looked to me as if they had stopped trying. Our tomato plants had grown fastest in the hottest weeks of summer, so I moved the two front jars to the shelf above the radiator, where my mother dries mittens. The third jar, half hidden behind the curtain, I left where it was. I pictured Hana coming home to crystals twice their size.

At seven she lifted the first skewer and stopped. The blocky crystals had gone soft at the corners, and the biggest one had slid off into the bottom of the jar, where it lay rounded like a sucked candy. The second skewer was nearly bare. She touched the side of the jar, and then she looked at the radiator, and then at me. I stood by the refrigerator, my stomach tight, and waited for her to shout.

"They were on the windowsill," she said.

I told her. It took about four sentences, and she wrote nothing down while I talked.

Then she opened the notebook to its first page, where she had copied a line from a library book, and read it aloud: warm water can hold more dissolved sugar than cold water. She read it twice. She went to the curtain and lifted out the third skewer. Its crystals were sharp-edged and a little longer than the night before.

"So this one is the control," she said, mostly to herself.

She worked until eleven. She measured all three skewers, stood the kitchen thermometer in each jar, and wrote the temperatures beside the lengths. Then she brought the poster board in from the hallway, and under the old title she taped a strip of paper with a second question in marker: "And What Makes Them Shrink?"

"What time did you move them?" she asked, pen raised.

"The bus gets in at three-thirty. So about three-forty."

She wrote it down: jars 1 and 2 moved to radiator, 3:40 p.m. Then she handed me the ruler and told me to hold it steady while she drew the graph, because the line for Wednesday was going to go down, and she wanted it straight.

My grandmother painted her workshop wall
the color of weak tea, and then, with a thin brush,
traced around each tool before she hung it up:
the hammer, the handsaw, three chisels in a row,
the level with its bubble in a green glass eye.

So when a tool is out, its shape stays on the wall,
a black line holding nothing,
the way a pillow keeps the hollow of a head
for a minute after the sleeper rises.

At the end of each day she walks the length of the wall
and fills every shape, and if one stays empty
she can say its name before she has looked,
the way you know which tooth is gone.

The summer I was twelve I borrowed the hammer
to build a raft at the mill pond,
and the pond kept it. I saw it go down
through the brown water, turning once,
and I dove for it until my lips went blue.

For the rest of August the outline hung there,
a hammer drawn around a hammer of bare wall.
She said nothing about it. Each evening
her hand went up to it, and came back.

In September I spent my lawn-mowing money
on a new one, yellow-handled,
a little shorter than hers had been,
and I hung it in the empty shape.

It almost fits. Around the head
a thin margin of the old line shows,
and below the handle a short stripe of black
where the longer one used to reach.

She could have painted it out. She has the brush,
and the tea-colored paint is still on the shelf.
She left the line as it was instead,
so now the wall holds two hammers:

the one I bought and the one I lost,
and every evening she checks them both
with a single touch of her hand.

traced around each tool before she hung it up:
the hammer, the handsaw, three chisels in a row,

and fills every shape, and if one stays empty

and the pond kept it. I saw it go down
through the brown water, turning once,
and I dove for it until my lips went blue.

a hammer drawn around a hammer of bare wall.

The summer I turned eleven, my father and I drove his pickup nine hundred miles to my grandmother's farm to bring back her upright piano. It took three days to get there, with two nights in motels along the way. The truck's radio worked only on hills, and the windows stayed down the whole time, so we talked loudly or kept quiet.

Before we left, he bought a road map at a gas station and handed it to me. "You're the navigator," he said. That meant calling out the route numbers before each turn and, every evening, drawing a small pencil circle around the place where we had stopped for the night.

I took the job seriously. I learned that red lines were highways, that thin gray lines were smaller roads that might be paved or might be gravel, and that the tiny numbers between two dots gave the miles between towns. Once, outside a city, I called an exit a mile too late, and we circled back through a neighborhood of warehouses while my father hummed and said that was how you saw a place.

I learned, too, that a road map opens easily and closes only under protest. Each time I unfolded it to find our place, it came back together in a new way, bulging, with the wrong state on the outside and creases running in new places. By the second morning it was as soft as cloth. My father watched me fight with it at a rest stop and told me that nobody in history had ever refolded a road map correctly.

On the last afternoon a sign warned of construction ahead, and I found a gray line that ran beside the highway and rejoined it forty miles on. My father studied it for a long moment, then took the exit. The gray road was gravel. It ran through two towns smaller than their names on the map and past a stand where a girl was selling peaches from the back of a car. We bought a bag and ate them over the dashboard, and we reached the farm an hour later than we would have, with juice on the steering wheel. That night I drew the third circle.

My father kept the map. Years later, when I was packing for college, he handed it to me in an envelope. The three circles were still there, faint and gray. But what I noticed was the creases. In a few places the paper was worn nearly through, and when I held it up to the window, light came through in small patches.

The patches were the places my thumbs had pressed while I looked: the warehouse exit, the gray road, the farm. I had spent that whole trip trying to fold the map back the way it had been sold. All along, it had been keeping its own record of where we had been, in the only way paper can.

Before we left, he bought a road map at a gas station and handed it to me. "You're the navigator," he said. That meant calling out the route numbers before each turn and, every evening, drawing a small pencil circle around the place where we had stopped for the night.

I took the job seriously. I learned that red lines were highways, that thin gray lines were smaller roads that might be paved or might be gravel, and that the tiny numbers between two dots gave the miles between towns. Once, outside a city, I called an exit a mile too late, and we circled back through a neighborhood of warehouses while my father hummed and said that was how you saw a place.

I learned, too, that a road map opens easily and closes only under protest. Each time I unfolded it to find our place, it came back together in a new way, bulging, with the wrong state on the outside and creases running in new places. By the second morning it was as soft as cloth. My father watched me fight with it at a rest stop and told me that nobody in history had ever refolded a road map correctly.

On the last afternoon a sign warned of construction ahead, and I found a gray line that ran beside the highway and rejoined it forty miles on. My father studied it for a long moment, then took the exit. The gray road was gravel. It ran through two towns smaller than their names on the map and past a stand where a girl was selling peaches from the back of a car. We bought a bag and ate them over the dashboard, and we reached the farm an hour later than we would have, with juice on the steering wheel. That night I drew the third circle.

My father kept the map. Years later, when I was packing for college, he handed it to me in an envelope. The three circles were still there, faint and gray. But what I noticed was the creases. In a few places the paper was worn nearly through, and when I held it up to the window, light came through in small patches.

The patches were the places my thumbs had pressed while I looked: the warehouse exit, the gray road, the farm. I had spent that whole trip trying to fold the map back the way it had been sold. All along, it had been keeping its own record of where we had been, in the only way paper can.

There is a familiar piece of advice given to young people, usually by adults who mean well: pick something and stick with it. The argument goes like this. Mastery takes thousands of hours, the hours have to start somewhere, and every year spent dabbling is a year your rivals spent practicing. A twelve-year-old who has played only tennis since the age of six, the argument concludes, will beat a twelve-year-old who has played six different sports.

That is probably true, at twelve. The trouble is that most of life is not a tennis match at twelve.

Early focus pays best in activities with fixed rules and quick, clear feedback. A tennis ball lands in or out; a scale on the piano is played correctly or it is not. In fields like these, the sooner the hours begin, the sooner they add up. But much of what people end up doing, such as running a business, teaching, writing, or designing a bridge, has rules that shift and feedback that arrives late. In those fields, a person who has seen many kinds of problems often has the advantage, because a solution borrowed from one place can be put to work in another.

There is also a simpler problem with choosing early: a ten-year-old is choosing with very little information. My cousin began the violin at four and practiced every day for eleven years. At fifteen she discovered the robotics club at her school and found that she would rather build things than play them. She was a good violinist. She was, by her own account, a happier engineer. Those eleven years were hardly wasted, since she still plays and says the practice taught her patience, but she arrived at the thing that suited her late, and only by accident.

Sampling has costs of its own, and they should be admitted. A person who tries everything and stays with each thing for a month may reach twenty with a closet full of abandoned equipment and no skill deep enough to enjoy. Depth matters. Some pleasures are open only to people who have pushed past the beginner's stage.

So the sensible course, it seems to me, is to treat the early years as a period of search rather than commitment: try widely, notice what keeps drawing you back, and then go deep. A late choice made with good information is usually better than an early one made with almost none. And the adult who tells you to pick one thing deserves a fair question in return: how many things they tried before they found theirs.

The Tamsen River had flooded the town of Corley before, but never the way it did in April of 1889. After nine days of rain, the water rose eleven feet in a single night and spread across the low ground east of Main Street, where the tannery, the lumberyard, and about forty houses stood. By morning people were rowing boats down Water Street. When the river went back, it left a line of brown mud on the walls of the bank building, chest-high, which the bank's owner had painted around in white so that the town would remember it.

The town council voted that summer to build a levee. The work took two years. When it was finished, the earthen wall ran for a mile and a half along the river's east bank, twelve feet high at its tallest point, with a path along its top where families walked on Sunday evenings. The county engineer, a woman named Ida Rusk, designed it to hold back a flood as high as the one of 1889, with two feet to spare.

What happened next is a pattern that historians of rivers have noticed in many places. The low ground behind the levee, which had been pasture and scattered houses, began to look safe. Within fifteen years the council had sold building lots there, and a school, a church, a hotel, and nearly two hundred houses had gone up on land the river had covered in 1889. Rusk wrote twice to the council asking that the lowest blocks be kept as open fields. "The levee was built for the last flood," she wrote in the second letter. "The river is under no obligation to repeat it." Her letters were read into the minutes and filed.

In March of 1913, after a warm rain fell on deep snow upstream, the Tamsen rose higher than anyone in Corley had seen. It reached the top of the levee near the tannery, poured over, and cut a gap forty feet wide. The water that came through moved more slowly than the flood of 1889, but it had far more to destroy. The damage that spring was several times greater than in 1889.

The levee was repaired, and raised, and it still stands. But the town did one thing differently afterward. Over the next decade the blocks nearest the river were bought back and turned into a park, the one people in Corley now call the Low Field. In its center stands a post painted with two lines. The lower one marks 1889. The upper one, three feet higher, marks 1913, and beside it someone has added a small brass plate with Ida Rusk's name.

The town council voted that summer to build a levee. The work took two years. When it was finished, the earthen wall ran for a mile and a half along the river's east bank, twelve feet high at its tallest point, with a path along its top where families walked on Sunday evenings. The county engineer, a woman named Ida Rusk, designed it to hold back a flood as high as the one of 1889, with two feet to spare.

What happened next is a pattern that historians of rivers have noticed in many places. The low ground behind the levee, which had been pasture and scattered houses, began to look safe. A glacier looks like the stillest thing on earth. Stand beside one for an afternoon and you will see nothing move except meltwater and the occasional falling stone. Yet nearly every glacier is flowing downhill, and over thousands of years that slow motion can reshape a mountain range.

A glacier begins where more snow falls each winter than melts each summer. Year after year the snow piles up, and the weight of the upper layers presses the lower ones first into dense, grainy ice and finally into solid glacial ice. Once the ice is thick enough, it begins to move under its own weight.

It moves in two ways. First, the ice itself deforms. Under enough pressure, the crystals that make up glacial ice slowly slip and change shape, so that the whole mass creeps downhill rather like very stiff dough. Only the upper part of a glacier, roughly the top fifty meters, is too lightly loaded to flow this way; it stays brittle and cracks open into the deep fissures called crevasses as the ice beneath it moves. Second, where the base of a glacier is wet, the ice can slide over the ground on a thin film of meltwater.

Both motions are slow. Many glaciers flow somewhere between a few centimeters and a meter or so a day, though a few move much faster. The speed also varies from place to place within the ice. When observers drive a straight row of stakes across a glacier and return a year later, the row has bent into a curve, because the ice in the middle moves faster than the ice slowed by friction against the valley walls.

A moving glacier carves the land in two main ways. Meltwater seeps into cracks in the bedrock beneath it and freezes, and the ice then pulls loosened blocks of rock away as it moves, a process called plucking. Those rocks, frozen into the base of the glacier, are dragged along the ground like the grit on sandpaper, scraping the bedrock smooth and leaving long scratches that point in the direction the ice traveled. The fine powder ground off in this way often turns glacial streams a milky gray.

The results are easiest to see after the ice is gone. A river, cutting downward, tends to make a narrow valley shaped like a V. A glacier fills its whole valley and grinds at the sides as well as the floor, widening it into a broad U with steep walls. Where a small side glacier once joined a large one, its valley may now end high up the wall of the main valley, with a stream pouring over the edge as a waterfall. Geologists read these shapes the way a tracker reads footprints, and it is hard to stand in such a valley without marveling at the patience of what made it.

original_item.passage:
A glacier looks like the stillest thing on earth. Stand beside one for an afternoon and you will see nothing move except meltwater and the occasional falling stone. Yet nearly every glacier is flowing downhill, and over thousands of years that slow motion can reshape a mountain range.

A glacier begins where more snow falls each winter than melts each summer. Year after year the snow piles up, and the weight of the upper layers presses the lower ones first into dense, grainy ice and finally into solid glacial ice. Once the ice is thick enough, it begins to move under its own weight.

It moves in two ways. First, the ice itself deforms. Under enough pressure, the crystals that make up glacial ice slowly slip and change shape, so that the whole mass creeps downhill rather like very stiff dough. Only the upper part of a glacier, roughly the top fifty meters, is too lightly loaded to flow this way; it stays brittle and cracks open into the deep fissures called crevasses as the ice beneath it moves. Second, where the base of a glacier is wet, the ice can slide over the ground on a thin film of meltwater.

Both motions are slow. Many glaciers flow somewhere between a few centimeters and a meter or so a day, though a few move much faster. The speed also varies from place to place within the ice. When observers drive a straight row of stakes across a glacier and return a year later, the row has bent into a curve, because the ice in the middle moves faster than the ice slowed by friction against the valley walls.

A moving glacier carves the land in two main ways. Meltwater seeps into cracks in the bedrock beneath it and freezes, and the ice then pulls loosened blocks of rock away as it moves, a process called plucking. Those rocks, frozen into the base of the glacier, are dragged along the ground like the grit on sandpaper, scraping the bedrock smooth and leaving long scratches that point in the direction the ice traveled. The fine powder ground off in this way often turns glacial streams a milky gray.

The results are easiest to see after the ice is gone. A river, cutting downward, tends to make a narrow valley shaped like a V. A glacier fills its whole valley and grinds at the sides as well as the floor, widening it into a broad U with steep walls. Where a small side glacier once joined a large one, its valley may now end high up the wall of the main valley, with a stream pouring over the edge as a waterfall. Geologists read these shapes the way a tracker reads footprints, and it is hard to stand in such a valley without marveling at the patience of what made it.
